people.name: Aaron Hurst
people.bio: Co-founded Imperative in 2014 to measure purpose at work after a decade running the Taproot Foundation. The Purpose Economy (2014) argued that meaning is becoming the primary unit of economic value, replacing information.

people.name: adrienne maree brown
people.bio: Writer and facilitator whose Emergent Strategy drew from Octavia Butler to map how movements, communities, and change actually unfold — nonlinear, relational, and alive. Essential reading for anyone building cooperatively.
life_story: Born 1978 in El Paso, Texas. An organiser, writer, and facilitator who spent years working with the Ruckus Society and the Movement Strategy Center before turning to the question of how movements actually change — not in theory, but in the body.

She was literary executor for Octavia E. Butler and co-edited Octavia's Brood (2015), a collection of visionary fiction by movement writers. Her own Emergent Strategy (2017) reframed organising through the lens of complexity, fractals, and biomimicry — how small, adaptive practices scale into systemic change.

Pleasure Activism (2019) and Holding Change (2021) extended the work. She is one of the most widely read voices in contemporary organising precisely because she treats joy, rest, and attention to relationship as political practices, not luxuries.

people.name: Al Carter
people.bio: Inventor who built the first rebounding mini-trampoline for therapeutic use in 1975 and went on to research lymphatic stimulation for decades. The Miracle of Rebound Exercise (1979) is the foundational text for the rebounder field.

people.name: Alain de Botton
people.bio: Founder of The School of Life in 2008. Brought philosophy out of the academy and into everyday questions — architecture, love, work, anxiety — through essayistic books and a global classroom network.

people.name: Alan Watts
people.bio: The philosopher who brought Eastern wisdom to the West. Thousands of lectures freely available — start anywhere.
life_story: Alan Wilson Watts was born on 6 January 1915 in Britain. He worked as a philosopher, writer, and speaker, and came to focus on the relationship between Eastern thought and Western intellectual life. His writing addressed the meaning of priesthood alongside questions drawn from Zen Buddhism — a range that suggests a formation shaped by both religious and philosophical inquiry. Over his working life he took on the role of interpreter, making Eastern traditions legible to Western readers who had little prior grounding in them.

Watts became widely known as an interpreter and populariser of Eastern philosophy for a Western audience. His writing included direct treatments of Zen Buddhism and a sustained examination, in Psychotherapy East & West, of the dialogue between Eastern frameworks and Western therapeutic thought. That pairing drew readers from both traditions and helped move Eastern ideas into broader Western discourse. The work was consistent rather than sensational: a long effort to articulate, in terms Western readers could follow, ideas that had not originated there.

Watts died on 16 November 1973. The Alan Watts Organization has since been dedicated to the preservation and curation of his output. His recorded lectures remain in wide circulation, accessible to anyone who seeks them. The written work — spanning Zen Buddhism, the meaning of priesthood, and the boundaries between Eastern and Western psychological thought — continues to be read. The organisation's ongoing curation ensures that what he produced endures as a standing introduction to the traditions he spent his working life explaining.

people.name: Albert Hofmann
people.bio: Swiss chemist at Sandoz who synthesised LSD in 1938 and first experienced its effects on the 1943 'Bicycle Day' ride home. Spent the next sixty years arguing the molecule was a tool for consciousness, not a recreational drug.
life_story: Albert Hofmann was born in Baden, Switzerland, the eldest child of a factory toolmaker. He attended the University of Zürich from 1926, working to support his family while pursuing his central interest: the chemistry of plants and animals. He graduated in 1929 and received his doctorate in chemistry in 1930. He joined the pharmaceutical-chemical department of Sandoz Laboratories in Basel — later to become Novartis — where the applied study of naturally occurring compounds became the focus of his career.

In 1938, Hofmann became the first scientist to synthesise lysergic acid diethylamide — LSD. Five years later, in 1943, he accidentally absorbed a small quantity through his fingertips and discovered its powerful psychoactive effects. That unplanned encounter set the direction for decades of research and, eventually, fierce cultural and legislative controversy. He also synthesised psilocybin, identifying it as the active compound in certain mushrooms used in indigenous Mexican ritual, following fieldwork in southern Mexico. He eventually became director of Sandoz's natural products department.

Hofmann maintained that LSD had legitimate therapeutic value in psychoanalysis, but was openly critical of its appropriation by the 1960s counterculture, a phenomenon he held partly responsible for the compound's prohibition. He set out his position in LSD: My Problem Child, and co-authored Plants of the Gods alongside ethnobotanist Richard Evans Schultes. The pharmacological groundwork he laid — isolating psychoactive substances from natural sources and characterising their effects — continues to underpin current clinical research into psychedelic-assisted treatment for depression, anxiety, and trauma.

people.name: Aldo Leopold
people.bio: Wrote the 1949 essay collection A Sand County Almanac, posthumously published, where he laid out the 'land ethic' — the idea that soil, water, and other species belong to a moral community. The seed of modern conservation thinking.

people.name: Alejandro Junger
people.bio: Cardiologist who developed the Clean program after his own gut-health collapse during a New York residency. The 21-day elimination protocol he published in 2009 went on to be one of the most widely adopted functional-medicine cleanses in the US.

people.name: Alex Ross
people.bio: Music critic at The New Yorker since 1996 whose The Rest Is Noise (2007) told the story of twentieth-century classical music as a story about politics and place. Won the National Book Critics Circle Award and a MacArthur Fellowship the same year.

people.name: Alex Soojung-Kim Pang
people.bio: Stanford-based futurist who spent years researching how Darwin, Lin-Manuel Miranda, and others structured their working day. Rest (2016) argued that deliberate rest is what separates the merely productive from the genuinely creative.

people.name: Andreas Antonopoulos
people.bio: Educator and advocate whose Mastering Bitcoin and The Internet of Money books, together with his decades of talks, shaped how a generation understood Bitcoin's moral and technical architecture.
life_story: Born 1972 in London, raised in Greece, educated at University College London. Early career in information security. Came to Bitcoin in 2012 and quickly became its clearest public educator — precisely because he was never a founder, never held a major stake, and therefore had no coin to sell.

Mastering Bitcoin (2014) and The Internet of Money (four volumes, 2016–2019) are still the canonical technical and philosophical introductions to the space. He has given hundreds of talks, most available free on YouTube.

In 2017 the community, learning that he had never enriched himself from his advocacy, crowdfunded him nearly 100 BTC in gratitude. He used a portion of it to continue educating full-time, and remains one of the most credible voices in a field full of incentive-distorted ones.

people.name: Andrew Huberman
people.bio: Stanford neuroscientist whose Huberman Lab podcast translates research into practical tools for focus, sleep, and performance. The clearest bridge between the lab and the body in contemporary neuroscience media.
life_story: Born 1975 in Palo Alto, son of a Stanford physicist. BA, MA, PhD in neurobiology, then a postdoc at Stanford and independent lab work at UCSD. Returned to Stanford Medical School as a tenured professor, where he runs the Huberman Lab studying vision, fear, and neural regeneration.

In early 2021 he launched the Huberman Lab podcast, translating peer-reviewed neuroscience into protocols for sleep, focus, light exposure, breathing, and physical performance. By 2024 it was one of the most-downloaded science podcasts in the world.

His work is not without controversy — he is at once a research scientist and a media figure, a position most academics find uncomfortable. The core contribution is durable: a generation of listeners now knows what morning sunlight does to circadian rhythm.

people.name: Anita Moorjani
people.bio: Author of Dying to Be Me, whose recovery from end-stage cancer after a profound near-death experience became one of the most widely shared first-person accounts of what love and self-acceptance can do.
life_story: Born in Singapore in 1959 to Indian parents, raised in Hong Kong. Trilingual childhood, successful corporate career, a conventional life — until, in her early forties, she was diagnosed with stage-four lymphoma.

Four years of deterioration followed. On 2 February 2006, organs failing, she slipped into a coma. In her account of what happened next she moved into an expanded field of awareness in which she encountered her deceased father, a clear sense of the purpose of her life, and a choice of whether to return. She returned. Within five weeks every tumour in her body was gone; within a few months she was discharged.

Her medical records and physician statements are documented. Dying to Be Me (2012) became a New York Times bestseller. She speaks and writes from California now. The NDE literature is vast, but hers is one of the clearest and most reported cases in the modern record.

people.name: Anodea Judith
people.bio: Therapist and somatic teacher who has spent four decades mapping the chakra system onto Western developmental psychology. Wheels of Life (1987) and Eastern Body Western Mind (1996) are the field's standard cross-tradition references.

people.name: anonymous (traditional Sanskrit)
people.bio: Author of The Guru Gita.

people.name: Arizona Wilder
people.bio: Former high priestess and MK-Ultra survivor who conducted Illuminati rituals at the highest levels of global power. Her testimony — first recorded with David Icke in Revelations of a Mother Goddess (1999) — covers shapeshifting bloodlines, Satanic ceremony, and the hidden architecture of control. Unfiltered and unflinching.

people.name: Arthur Wellinger
people.bio: Swiss agricultural engineer who led the IEA Bioenergy Task on biogas for over twenty years. Co-edited The Biogas Handbook (2013), still the standard technical reference for anaerobic-digestion engineers in Europe and beyond.

people.name: B.K.S. Iyengar
people.bio: Studied with T. Krishnamacharya in Mysore in the 1930s, then built the precision-alignment school of yoga that bears his name. Light on Yoga (1966) catalogued 200 asanas with the photographic rigour that made him the West's most-translated yoga teacher of the twentieth century.

people.name: Balaji Srinivasan
people.bio: Technologist, investor, and author of The Network State — the foundational text on starting a new kind of country online before building its physical presence. His work maps the organising principle behind the Sanctuary pillar.
life_story: Born 1980 in Long Island to Indian immigrants — both physicians. Stanford: BS, MS, PhD, and MS in engineering, plus a stint teaching a popular class on statistics and data mining. Co-founded Counsyl (genomics) and then 21.co, which became Earn.com and was acquired by Coinbase in 2018.

Served as Coinbase's first CTO and as a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz. Became one of the most widely cited voices in crypto, longevity, and political futures — in part because he treats them as one field.

In 2022 he self-published The Network State, which argued that a new kind of polity could bootstrap online, build moral consensus, accumulate capital, and then negotiate physical territory. The book has become the organising principle behind a generation of experiments. FRQNCY's Sanctuary pillar is downstream of it.

people.name: Barbara Marciniak
people.bio: Barbara Marciniak has channeled a collective of multidimensional beings from the Pleiades star system since 1988. Her book Bringers of the Dawn is one of the most widely read channeled texts ever published — a dense, demanding transmission on DNA activation, timelines, and the game being played on Earth.

channels.name: The Pleiadians
channels.description: A collective of multidimensional beings from the Pleiades star system. Their transmissions through Barbara Marciniak since 1988 cover DNA activation, timelines, planetary awakening, and the deeper game being played on Earth — demanding, dense, and among the most widely read channeled material published.

life_story: Born in North Carolina. Trained as a teacher. In May 1988, during a trip to Athens and the ancient sites of Crete and Egypt, she began to channel a collective of beings who identified themselves as coming from the Pleiades.

The first book, Bringers of the Dawn (1992), is still one of the densest and most widely read channeled texts ever published — an account of Earth as a living library, a game being played across timelines, and the DNA activation said to be underway during this period of human history.

She has continued publishing and teaching for more than thirty years from her base in North Carolina. Earth, Family of Light, and Path of Empowerment extend the same transmission. Read her critically or read her as scripture; the material has shaped the esoteric conversation for a generation.

people.name: Benjamin Zander
people.bio: Conductor of the Boston Philharmonic since 1979 and a TED stage regular. Built his teaching practice around the conviction that every person in a room is already capable of greatness — the conductor's job is to invite it out.

people.name: Bertrand Russell
people.bio: British philosopher and mathematician, Nobel laureate 1950. His 1932 essay In Praise of Idleness argued that a four-hour workday would free humanity for thought, art, and joy — a century before the four-day-week debate finally caught up.
life_story: Bertrand Arthur William Russell was born on 18 May 1872. A British philosopher, logician, mathematician, historian, and social critic, he was one of the most wide-ranging intellectual figures of his century, rarely confining himself to a single discipline or register. By the late 1920s he was writing essayistic criticism on pressing social and political questions — fascism, communism, education, the shape of Western civilisation — building toward the sustained popular argument that would become his most widely read book.

In Praise of Idleness, published in 1935, collects essays composed between 1928 and 1933. The title piece, written in 1932, makes a direct and deliberately provocative case: that four hours of daily work is sufficient for any person, with the remaining hours freed for thought, conversation, and a fuller life. Around that central proposition, the book assembles broader arguments — on architecture and social planning, on the ancestry of fascism, on the case for socialism, on education and discipline, and on the relationship between stoicism and mental health.

Russell died on 2 February 1970, having lived to ninety-seven. The essays in In Praise of Idleness have remained in print. The argument on working hours — considered provocative in 1932 — found new audiences in later debates about shortened working weeks and the relationship between labour, leisure, and what a life well spent might look like. The book's wider character, its willingness to bring philosophy, economics, and social criticism together in plain prose, is the quality that has kept it circulating long after the circumstances that prompted it.

people.name: Bessel van der Kolk
people.bio: Dutch-American psychiatrist who spent four decades at Boston's Trauma Center showing that traumatic memory lives in the body, not the narrative. The Body Keeps the Score (2014) made somatic therapy mainstream.
life_story: Bessel van der Kolk was born in the Netherlands and built his clinical and research career in the United States, settling in Boston. From the 1970s he concentrated on post-traumatic stress, a field then poorly understood and frequently dismissed in mainstream psychiatry. Over three decades of working directly with survivors — veterans, abuse victims, and those who grew up in violent or chaotic households — he accumulated the clinical evidence and neurobiological data that would underpin his most influential work. He holds a professorship in psychiatry at Boston University School of Medicine.

In _The Body Keeps the Score_, van der Kolk drew on his own research and that of fellow specialists to argue that traumatic experience is not merely a psychological wound but a physiological one: it literally reshapes both brain and body, disrupting the systems that govern pleasure, engagement, self-control, and trust. The book examined treatments that go well beyond conventional talk therapy — neurofeedback, meditation, yoga, drama, sport — each working with the brain's neuroplasticity to open recovery routes the standard medical model had largely overlooked. Its publication shifted how trauma is understood and approached across psychiatry, psychology, and allied clinical fields.

Van der Kolk continues as president of the Trauma Research Foundation in Brookline, Massachusetts, where his work centres on trauma treatment development, clinician training, and ongoing research into how traumatic experience physically shapes the nervous system across the lifespan. _The Body Keeps the Score_ remains in wide circulation, consulted by clinicians, educators, social workers, and general readers alike. Its account of the body's central role in both holding and recovering from trauma has become a working reference across medicine, psychology, and education.

people.name: Bill Burnett
people.bio: Executive director of Stanford's Design Program who, with Dave Evans, adapted product-design methods into a popular course on building a life. Designing Your Life (2016) became the most-taken class in Stanford's continuing-studies catalogue.

people.name: Bill Kovach
people.bio: Former Washington bureau chief of the New York Times and founding chair of the Committee of Concerned Journalists in 1997. His Elements of Journalism distilled the craft to nine principles — truth, verification, independence — that still set the bar.

people.name: Bill Mollison
people.bio: Australian researcher who co-coined 'permaculture' with David Holmgren in 1978 and spent the next four decades teaching the design system worldwide. The 1988 Designers' Manual remains the field's foundational text.
life_story: Bill Mollison worked as a scientist, naturalist, and university professor before his mounting concern for the environment redirected his career. Over decades of observation and study he became a vigorous campaigner against environmental exploitation — a position that pushed him toward constructive rather than reactive work. Rather than remaining at the level of protest, he channelled his expertise into building a practical design framework for sustainable land use. That framework became permaculture: a discipline assembled from close attention to natural systems and the patterns they follow.

As founder and director of the Permaculture Institute, Mollison formalised and disseminated the discipline through teaching, fieldwork, and writing. His most thorough statement of the work, Permaculture: A Designers' Manual, set out its principles and methods in exhaustive detail and became a foundational reference for practitioners worldwide. The publication established permaculture not as ideological stance but as a rigorous design system applicable across climates — from dryland projects to urban city-farms and community-supported agriculture schemes across the United States, Europe, and Scandinavia.

Mollison's teaching extended from the Arctic through sub-tropical and equatorial regions, and he worked directly with Native Americans, Indigenous Australians, tribal communities of the Deccan and Kalahari, San groups, the Pima people of the Sonora, and seven Amazonian language groups, among others. Peoples of the Pacific, South East Asia, and South Africa engaged with his methods and carried them forward. He devoted his energies to designing sustainable systems, writing, and teaching across more than forty years of active concern for the environment. The discipline he built and the manual he wrote remain central to permaculture practice.

people.name: Bill Ryan & Kerry Cassidy
people.bio: Since 2006 they have filmed hundreds of hours of whistleblower testimony — insiders from intelligence, military, finance, and the fringes of science — and built Project Camelot into the internet's most important archive of voices the mainstream will not air.

people.name: Birgit Fischer
people.bio: Austrian medium, healer, and four-time SPIEGEL bestselling author — channels Starseed messages and galactic intelligences. One of the most prominent voices in German-language spiritual media.

people.name: Bob Burg
people.bio: Speaker and sales trainer whose 2007 parable The Go-Giver — co-written with John David Mann — sold over a million copies on the counter-intuitive claim that giving value first is the most reliable path to commercial success.

people.name: Bob Lazar
people.bio: The man who brought Area 51 and element 115 (moscovium) to public consciousness decades before its scientific confirmation. Official site.

people.name: Bob Roth
people.bio: CEO of the David Lynch Foundation since 2011 and a Transcendental Meditation teacher for over five decades. Has taught TM to hundreds of thousands of students at-risk youth, veterans, and inner-city public-school children — funded entirely through donations.

people.name: Brian Weiss
people.bio: Yale-trained psychiatrist and chair of psychiatry at Mount Sinai Miami when a hypnosis session with a patient in 1980 surfaced what appeared to be past-life memory. Many Lives, Many Masters (1988) made past-life regression a topic mainstream therapists could discuss.

people.name: Bruce Schneier
people.bio: The world's most respected security technologist. His cryptography work, books, and blog form the clearest voice in the field on how systems fail and how to secure them.
life_story: Born 1963 in New York City. Degrees in physics and computer science, then a long career at the intersection of cryptography, policy, and practice. Designed the Blowfish and Twofish ciphers. Wrote Applied Cryptography (1996), which was, for a decade, how cryptographers learned cryptography.

Has fellowships at Harvard Kennedy School and Harvard Berkman Klein Center. Serves on the boards of EFF and Access Now. Has been called the world's most respected security technologist by The Economist — a label he has done nothing to undermine.

His blog, Schneier on Security, has been running since 2004. His books — Secrets and Lies, Beyond Fear, Data and Goliath, Click Here to Kill Everybody — are required reading for anyone who cares how digital systems actually fail. The voice is patient, precise, and unintimidated by power.

people.name: Bruce Wiseman
people.bio: Former US president of the Citizens Commission on Human Rights and longtime critic of psychiatric over-prescription. His work argues that the chemical-imbalance model has been a marketing claim with thin scientific footing — a position now mainstream among many psychiatric researchers.

people.name: Camila Russo
people.bio: Former Bloomberg crypto reporter who founded The Defiant in 2019, the leading editorial outlet covering decentralised finance. The Infinite Machine traces Ethereum from Vitalik's whitepaper to the DeFi summer of 2020.
life_story: Camila Russo studied journalism at Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile before completing a Master of Science at Northwestern University's Medill School of Journalism. She began her career writing international news for El Mercurio, Chile's largest national newspaper, winning first place for online journalism from Brazil's exchange operator BM&F Bovespa. She then joined Bloomberg News, spending eight years reporting on emerging markets from Buenos Aires, European stocks from Madrid, and macro movements from New York — a cross-market grounding that positioned her, by 2017, as the outlet's first journalist to cover cryptocurrency as a daily beat.

Reporting on Argentina's recurring economic crises had sharpened her interest in Bitcoin as an alternative store of value, and daily crypto coverage deepened her focus on Ethereum. When Bloomberg declined her proposal to launch a dedicated crypto team, Russo left to write The Infinite Machine (HarperCollins, 2020), the first book-length account of Ethereum's founding. Drawing on more than a hundred interviews, it traced Vitalik Buterin's conception of the platform and followed the coalition of coders who built it through speculative frenzy, regulatory scrutiny, and internal conflict.

Before publication, Russo had already founded The Defiant — a media platform covering decentralised finance, launched in June 2019. It grew into a multi-channel company publishing news, analysis, and a podcast for readers navigating the DeFi space. She has continued as its founder and chief executive. The Infinite Machine remains the primary journalistic record of Ethereum's early years, and The Defiant continues to document the ecosystem the book introduced to a wider audience.

people.name: Carl Jung
people.bio: Swiss psychiatrist who broke with Freud in 1913 to develop analytical psychology — the collective unconscious, archetypes, individuation. His 1952 essay on synchronicity reframed meaningful coincidence as a category as real as causality.

people.name: Carl Sagan
people.bio: The cosmologist, science communicator, and author whose Cosmos series and writing (Pale Blue Dot, The Demon-Haunted World) shaped how a generation understood our place in the universe. Science infused with awe, advocacy for reason delivered with poetry.
life_story: Born 1934 in Brooklyn to a working-class Jewish family. Chicago, Harvard, Cornell — he became the rare scientist who was also a public poet. He served as astronomy's bridge to the general mind for thirty years.

He helped NASA design the plaques on Pioneer 10 and 11 and chaired the committee that assembled the Voyager Golden Record — humanity's message to anyone who might find it. In 1980 his Cosmos PBS series reached 500 million viewers in sixty countries. In 1994 he wrote the Pale Blue Dot passage that is still the most widely shared cosmological prose in English.

He died of pneumonia in December 1996, aged 62, after two years with myelodysplasia. His last book, The Demon-Haunted World, is his warning to the century after him: science is a candle in the dark, and the dark is patient.

people.name: Carlo Rovelli
people.bio: Italian theoretical physicist working at the edges of loop quantum gravity and the philosophy of time. His short books (Seven Brief Lessons on Physics, The Order of Time) are among the most beautiful introductions to modern physics ever written.
life_story: Born 1956 in Verona. A physicist who came of age politically in the 1970s — part of Italy's counterculture, with a police file to show for it — before settling into the most abstract problem he could find: what space and time actually are.

He is one of the founders of loop quantum gravity, an approach that tries to quantise gravity itself, and has spent decades working between Italy, the US, and France at the Centre de Physique Théorique in Marseille.

His Seven Brief Lessons on Physics began as a series of newspaper columns for an Italian weekend paper. Translated into more than forty languages, it sold over a million copies — proof that people still want to read about the universe when it is written beautifully.

people.name: Carmine Gallo
people.bio: Communications coach who has spent twenty years studying TED talks frame-by-frame. Talk Like TED (2014) reverse-engineered the nine elements that distinguish the most-watched talks from the millions that never break a hundred views.

people.name: Carol Sanford
people.bio: Spent five decades advising companies including Google, DuPont and Seventh Generation on regenerative practice. Her work treats business as a living system whose purpose is to evolve the ecosystems it touches, not merely extract from them.

people.name: Charles F. Haanel
people.bio: American businessman who in 1912 published The Master Key System as a 24-part correspondence course on focused attention and creative thought. An early New Thought text that quietly shaped Napoleon Hill and the modern manifestation lineage.

people.name: Charles Fillmore
people.bio: Co-founded the Unity School of Christianity with his wife Myrtle in Kansas City in 1889 after Myrtle's spontaneous remission from tuberculosis. Prosperity (1936) extended New Thought principles into the financial life of his Unity students.

people.name: Chetan Parkyn
people.bio: Author of Human Design — Understanding the Mechanics of Your Inner Universe.

people.name: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie
people.bio: Nigerian novelist whose 2009 TED talk The Danger of a Single Story has been viewed over forty million times. Half of a Yellow Sun (2006) and Americanah (2013) brought the Igbo-diaspora experience into the global literary mainstream.
life_story: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie grew up in Nigeria. Before her novels appeared, her shorter work had already found its way into significant international outlets — The New Yorker, Granta, The O. Henry Prize Stories, the Financial Times, and Zoetrope — establishing her as a writer operating well outside regional margins. Her debut novel, Purple Hibiscus, confirmed the reach of her ambition, winning both the Commonwealth Writers' Prize and the Hurston/Wright Legacy Award.

Half of a Yellow Sun, her second novel, won the Orange Prize and was named a National Book Critics Circle Award finalist and a New York Times Notable Book. A story collection, The Thing Around Your Neck, extended her work in shorter form. In 2013, Americanah followed two young Nigerians — Ifemelu and Obinze — across continents, using Ifemelu's years in the United States to examine race and identity from an African vantage. The novel won the National Book Critics Circle Award for Fiction and the Chicago Tribune Heartland Prize, and was named one of the New York Times Ten Best Books of the Year.

Adichie's work has been translated into thirty languages. Her writing has appeared consistently across major international publications, and her four books — Purple Hibiscus, Half of a Yellow Sun, The Thing Around Your Neck, and Americanah — remain in broad circulation. The body of work she has produced maps Nigerian life, the African diaspora, and the negotiation of identity across migration in a way that has reached readers across dozens of countries and language traditions.

people.name: Chris Anderton
people.bio: Senior Lecturer at Solent University and author of Music Festivals in the UK (Routledge, 2018). Researches festival cultures, popular music, and the economy of live events.

people.name: Chris Goodall
people.bio: British economist and clean-energy investor who edits Carbon Commentary, a sector-defining newsletter on the energy transition since 2007. The Switch argued that solar would out-compete fossil fuels on price alone — and it did.

people.name: Chris Voss
people.bio: FBI lead international hostage negotiator from 2003 to 2007 who worked over 150 kidnappings before founding the Black Swan Group. Never Split the Difference (2016) translates hostage-room tactics — mirroring, labelling, calibrated questions — into everyday negotiation.

people.name: Christopher Alexander
people.bio: Architect at Berkeley whose 1977 A Pattern Language and 1979 Timeless Way of Building proposed that good design can be reduced to a vocabulary of 253 reusable patterns. The work seeded modern software design patterns, wiki culture, and the agile movement.

people.name: Claude M. Bristol
people.bio: American journalist and Marine veteran whose 1948 The Magic of Believing distilled thirty years of practical research into how concentrated thought translates into action. A precursor text to nearly every visualisation book that followed.

people.name: Coleman Barks
people.bio: Poet and former English professor at Georgia who, working from John Moyne's literal translations, rendered Rumi into the colloquial American English that made the thirteenth-century Sufi poet the best-selling poet in the United States by the 1990s.

people.name: Colin Beavan
people.bio: Spent a year with his family in Manhattan attempting to produce zero net environmental impact — no electricity, no taxis, no packaging, no elevators. No Impact Man (2009) is the field-journal of the experiment and made low-footprint living a documentary subject.

people.name: Curtis Stone
people.bio: Built a quarter-acre commercial vegetable farm in Kelowna, British Columbia that grossed six figures annually, then taught the method to thousands through The Urban Farmer (2015). Made small-plot intensive growing financially serious.

people.name: Dale Carnegie
people.bio: Author of How to Win Friends and Influence People — the 1936 text on human relations that has sold over 30 million copies and remains the foundation of nearly every communication-skills book written since.
life_story: Born 1888 on a Missouri farm, one of four children in a poor family. Warrensburg State Teachers College, then a string of jobs — sales, a stint in Nebraska peddling bacon and soap, a failed attempt at acting — before he landed on the thing he was actually good at: teaching public speaking at the YMCA in New York City.

The classes became legendary. He wrote textbooks for them. In 1936, drawing on fifteen years of teaching and the stories his students told, he published How to Win Friends and Influence People. It has sold over thirty million copies and, nearly a century later, still sits on most lists of the most influential books of the twentieth century.
He died in 1955. The institute he founded continues to teach his method on six continents. Almost every communication-skills book written since owes him something.

people.name: Daniel Levitin
people.bio: Cognitive neuroscientist at McGill who spent the 1980s as a record producer for Stevie Wonder and Steely Dan before turning to research. This Is Your Brain on Music (2006) was the first serious popular account of how music shapes the brain.
life_story: Daniel J. Levitin's path to neuroscience ran through the recording studio. Before entering academia, he worked as a session musician, sound engineer, and record producer — accumulating a working knowledge of music-making from the inside. That professional grounding, rare among researchers, shaped the questions he would later bring to the laboratory: not merely how music is structured, but what happens in the brain of someone who plays, records, and listens. The dual vantage point — industry and institution — became the foundation of his research.

His book This Is Your Brain on Music brought those questions to a wide audience. The work examines music — its composition, its performance, the mechanics of listening, and the reasons we enjoy it — through the lens of neuroscience. Drawing on both laboratory research and his years working in the recording industry, Levitin addressed how the brain processes sound and constructs the experience we call music. The book reframed the subject not as a purely cultural matter, but as something rooted in the biology of perception.

At McGill University, Levitin holds the Bell Chair in the Psychology of Electronic Communication and runs the Laboratory for Musical Perception, Cognition and Expertise. He has written for scientific journals and music trade publications including Grammy and Billboard, remaining active in both fields. His work continues at the intersection of cognitive science and music, and the laboratory he established at McGill stands as one of the field's dedicated centres for understanding what music does to the human mind.

people.name: Darryl Anka
people.bio: Darryl Anka has channeled Bashar since 1983 — teachings on parallel realities, permission slips, and following your highest excitement.

channels.name: Bashar
channels.description: A multi-dimensional being from a future Earth timeline, channeled by Darryl Anka since 1983. Bashar's teachings center on parallel realities, permission slips, and the practice of following your highest excitement in every moment — one of the most accessible and pragmatic transmissions in contemporary channeling.

people.name: Dave Evans
people.bio: Co-founder of Electronic Arts who left tech to teach design thinking at Stanford alongside Bill Burnett. Designing Your Life (2016) is the book version of the most popular class in Stanford's continuing-studies catalogue.

people.name: David Baxter
people.bio: Bioenergy researcher who led the IEA Bioenergy Task 37 working group with Arthur Wellinger and co-edited The Biogas Handbook (2013), the standard technical reference for anaerobic-digestion engineers.

people.name: David Bohm
people.bio: Theoretical physicist who worked with Einstein at Princeton and later proposed the 'implicate order' — a universe in which every part contains the whole. His late-life dialogue practice influenced everything from organisational development to Krishnamurti.

people.name: David Cameron Gikandi
people.bio: Kenyan author and consultant who worked on the film What the Bleep Do We Know!?. His 2008 book reframed wealth-building as an inner state — perception, gratitude, and identity — rather than a series of external transactions.

people.name: David Deutsch
people.bio: Oxford physicist who in 1985 wrote the paper defining the universal quantum computer — the theoretical foundation every quantum machine since has been built on. The Fabric of Reality (1997) joins quantum theory, evolution, computation, and epistemology into one explanatory frame.

people.name: David Flynn
people.bio: American researcher and amateur archaeologist who spent years studying the geometry of Mars's Cydonia region. Cydonia: The Secret Chronicles of Mars (2002) is the closest thing the field has to a primary text, even where the conclusions remain contested.

people.name: David Graeber
people.bio: Anthropologist at LSE and one of the intellectual architects of Occupy Wall Street, where he is credited with coining 'we are the 99%'. Co-wrote The Dawn of Everything (2021) with David Wengrow shortly before his sudden death — a sweeping rewrite of human prehistory.
life_story: David Rolfe Graeber was born on 12 February 1961. He trained as an anthropologist and joined Yale University in 1998, specialising in theories of value and social theory. Over nearly a decade as assistant then associate professor, he built the intellectual foundations that would inform his later books. When Yale chose not to renew his position ahead of a tenure decision — a move that prompted a petition signed by more than 4,500 academics — he moved to Goldsmiths, University of London, serving as Reader in Social Anthropology from 2007 to 2013, before joining the London School of Economics as a professor.

His book Debt: The First 5,000 Years (2011) argued that debt — not barter — was the original medium of human exchange, and that credit arrangements predated coined money by millennia. The argument reframed conventional economic history and reached a wide readership well beyond academic circles. Subsequent work extended the critique: The Utopia of Rules (2015) examined bureaucracy as a form of structural coercion, while Bullshit Jobs: A Theory (2018) made the case that a significant proportion of modern employment serves no meaningful purpose — social or productive.

Graeber died on 2 September 2020. The Dawn of Everything, published posthumously, extended his career-long questioning of settled assumptions about human society and history. Throughout his life he combined scholarship with anarchist activism, declining to separate the two. His books remain in print and widely assigned in anthropology, economics, and political theory; his arguments about debt, labour, and the nature of work continue to be discussed in and well beyond academic life.

people.name: David Hoffman
people.bio: Co-founder of Bankless with Ryan Sean Adams. His clear explanations of Ethereum's economic architecture and long-term thesis have made Bankless the primary education source for the bankless generation.
life_story: Born and raised in North Carolina. Trained in software and crypto economics. Co-founded Bankless with Ryan Sean Adams in 2019 — at first a podcast and newsletter, now one of the most-cited media brands in the Ethereum ecosystem.

Hoffman is the one most likely, on any given episode, to explain why a protocol matters at the level of monetary premium and long-term economic architecture. His framing of ETH as money, as a productive asset, and as the foundation of a parallel financial system, has shaped how a generation of investors thinks about the space.
Bankless has grown into a full media company, an investment DAO, and an education platform. Hoffman's long-form essays remain the clearest writing in the business.

people.name: David J. Schwartz
people.bio: Professor of marketing at Georgia State and longtime motivational speaker whose 1959 Magic of Thinking Big has sold over six million copies. One of the first books to argue that the size of a person's results is set by the size of their thinking.

people.name: David Kushner
people.bio: American journalist whose Masters of Doom (2003) chronicled John Carmack and John Romero building id Software in a Texas apartment and inventing the first-person shooter. The defining narrative of modern game development.

people.name: David Montgomery
people.bio: Geologist at the University of Washington whose research on soil traced civilisations rising and falling with topsoil health. Growing a Revolution (2017) profiled the farmers reversing that decline through cover crops and no-till.

people.name: David Wallace-Wells
people.bio: Climate columnist at the New York Times whose 2017 New York magazine essay 'The Uninhabitable Earth' broke through climate-coverage politeness. Expanded into a 2019 book that became the genre's commercial benchmark.

people.name: David Wengrow
people.bio: Professor of comparative archaeology at UCL who co-wrote The Dawn of Everything (2021) with David Graeber. Used decades of new digs to overturn the standard story of human history — that hierarchy was inevitable once we stopped foraging.

people.name: David Zilber
people.bio: Headed the fermentation lab at Noma in Copenhagen from 2014 to 2018. Co-wrote The Noma Guide to Fermentation (2018) with René Redzepi — the most rigorous popular fermentation book ever published and a standard text in restaurant kitchens worldwide.

people.name: Deepak Chopra
people.bio: Indian-American physician, teacher, and author whose work across dozens of books has brought yoga, Ayurveda, and consciousness into mainstream Western self-development.
life_story: Deepak Chopra is an Indian-American physician whose career moved progressively away from conventional medical practice and towards the intersection of Ayurveda, consciousness studies, and alternative medicine. That reorientation became the foundation for a substantial body of teaching and writing. Drawing on Indian philosophical traditions and reframing them for Western readers, he developed a working framework for understanding health and human potential that placed the relationship between mind, body, and natural law at its centre, and built his output around communicating that framework in accessible terms.

*The Seven Spiritual Laws of Success* distils his core teachings into seven principles governing natural law and human potential, arguing that sustainable success arises from alignment with one's own nature rather than from effort or ambition alone. The book became a touchstone of the self-development genre, carrying his central argument—that wellbeing, health, and material abundance can coexist—into mainstream circulation. Across dozens of subsequent books, he continued to map the ground between medicine, consciousness, and Ayurvedic practice.

Chopra has remained an active teacher and public speaker, continuing to write and extend his work into new formats. His first dedicated yoga course, *Yoga: Your Body as a Field of Awareness*, applies his long-standing focus on consciousness and bodily awareness to structured practice. His output spans alternative medicine, self-development, and consciousness studies, and his books remain in print and widely circulated. The teaching continues across books, courses, and public engagements, and the framework he built over decades holds a settled place in mainstream self-development.

people.name: Dexter Yager
people.bio: Amway distributor who built one of the largest direct-sales organisations in the company's history and trained thousands through cassette tapes and rallies starting in the 1970s. Becoming Rich captures his ground-level method for building people-led businesses.

people.name: Dolores Cannon
people.bio: Hypnotherapist, past-life regressionist, and founder of Quantum Healing Hypnosis Technique (QHHT). Across 50 years and tens of thousands of sessions she assembled one of the most coherent bodies of channeled material on Earth — Nostradamus, Jesus, starseeds, the volunteer souls, and the shift into the New Earth. Read her or don't, but you can't study this field without her.
life_story: Born 1931 in St. Louis. A Navy wife who in the late 1960s discovered, alongside her husband Johnny, that regression hypnosis could take subjects into something far stranger than past lives. For the next fifty years she refined her method.

In the late 1970s she developed Quantum Healing Hypnosis Technique (QHHT), a protocol for contacting what she called the Subconscious — a layer of a person that appeared to hold information about past lives, future lives, the body's healing, and the broader structure of reality. She trained thousands of practitioners worldwide.

Across seventeen books — Conversations with Nostradamus, Jesus and the Essenes, The Convoluted Universe, The Three Waves of Volunteers — she assembled one of the most coherent bodies of channeled material ever published by a single researcher. She died in 2014 at 83. QHHT continues.

people.name: Don Norman
people.bio: Cognitive scientist who coined 'user experience' while at Apple in the early 1990s, then co-founded the Nielsen Norman Group. The Design of Everyday Things (1988) is still the entry text for anyone designing anything anyone uses.

people.name: Donella Meadows
people.bio: Lead author of the 1972 Limits to Growth report that first modelled planetary overshoot, and founder of the Sustainability Institute. Thinking in Systems was assembled from her drafts after her 2001 death and remains the clearest introduction to systems thinking in print.
life_story: Donella Meadows was an American environmental scientist, teacher, and writer who became an early voice in systems analysis at MIT and in broader research circles — bringing scientific rigour to a field still finding its shape. Her dual grounding in environmental science and systems thinking positioned her to address questions that cut across ecology, economics, and governance, and her work as a teacher ran alongside her research throughout her career.

Her most enduring contribution is Thinking in Systems, a clear, wide-reaching account of how complex systems behave, in theory and in practice. Meadows wrote with an elegance and accessibility rare in technical work, connecting careful descriptions of systems analysis to their personal, social, societal, and political implications. The book drew readers who would never have approached a formal systems text and gave the field a vocabulary that crossed disciplinary lines.

Meadows did not live to see the book in print; it was completed from a draft manuscript after her death and released posthumously. Her reputation as both researcher and communicator meant it reached well beyond specialist circles, and it has continued to circulate across decades, drawing in readers from science, policy, and public life who might otherwise never have met the subject. Thinking in Systems remains the entry point through which many people first encounter the discipline she helped establish.

people.name: Donna Eden
people.bio: Recovered from multiple sclerosis in the 1970s through what she came to call energy medicine — a practice combining acupressure, meridian work, and chakra balancing. Has since trained over 100,000 practitioners through her school.
life_story: From childhood, Donna Eden could perceive the body's energy fields directly — a capacity that determined the direction of her life. Where others might have treated this as a purely personal faculty, she worked to understand what she was seeing and to develop a system that could be taught to others. That system drew on traditions comparable to acupressure and therapeutic touch, and over time became the foundation of her career as a teacher and practitioner of energy medicine.

Her primary contribution is Energy Medicine, co-authored with her husband David Feinstein. The book presents a methodical framework for working with the body's energy systems to support health and wellbeing, and has been translated into twelve languages. Through workshops and live presentations, Eden has taught around fifty thousand people worldwide how to apply its techniques. Carolyn Myss described it as one of the foundational studies for holistic medicine — a standing it has maintained as the field developed.

Eden has continued to teach internationally, her sessions noted for audience participation and live demonstration of the techniques laid out in her book. The central move of her career — translating a personal perceptual ability into a structured, repeatable methodology — is what allowed her work to travel at scale, reaching practitioners across disciplines. Energy Medicine remains in wide circulation across twelve languages and stands as the primary introductory text for the field.

people.name: Doug Wead
people.bio: Former special assistant to George H.W. Bush who later wrote biographies of the Bush family and interviewed billionaires across industries. Becoming Rich pulled themes from those conversations into a study of how dynastic wealth gets built.

people.name: Douglas Hofstadter
people.bio: Distinguished professor at Indiana University whose 1979 Gödel, Escher, Bach won the Pulitzer for its argument that consciousness emerges from self-referential loops — the strange loops that mathematics, music, and visual paradox all share.
life_story: Douglas Hofstadter is an American scholar whose work sits at the intersection of cognitive science, physics, and comparative literature. His research has long centred on questions that resist easy disciplinary framing: how a mind builds a sense of self in relation to the world around it, how analogy-making drives both artistic and mathematical discovery, and what the structure of formal systems can tell us about the nature of consciousness. These concerns — accumulated across decades of inquiry — converged in the work that brought him wide attention.

In 1979 Hofstadter published *Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid*, an ambitious inquiry into formal systems and the conditions under which consciousness and meaning might emerge from them. The book argued that self-referential loops — structures that fold back and represent themselves — offer a model for how mind arises from matter, and wove that argument through mathematics, music, and visual art. It won the Pulitzer Prize for general nonfiction and a National Book Award for Science, and brought questions of machine intelligence and consciousness to a wide general readership.

Hofstadter returned to the core questions of *GEB* in *I Am a Strange Loop* (2007), which won the *Los Angeles Times* Book Prize for Science and Technology. His research has continued to address analogy-making, artistic creation, literary translation, and the nature of discovery in mathematics and physics. *Gödel, Escher, Bach* endures as a foundational text in cognitive science — an unusually sustained attempt to map the territory between formal systems and the emergence of mind, and one that continues to shape how those questions are framed.

people.name: Dr. David R. Hawkins
people.bio: Psychiatrist and spiritual teacher who mapped the calibrated levels of human consciousness — from shame at the bottom to enlightenment at the top. His kinesiology research revealed that love and truth calibrate exponentially higher than fear and force. Essential for anyone serious about the mechanics of vibration.
life_story: Born 1927 in Milwaukee. A psychiatrist who ran one of the largest clinical practices in New York for decades, treating everyone from celebrities to lifelong schizophrenics. Co-authored Orthomolecular Psychiatry with Linus Pauling in 1973. Conventional, credentialed, and then something broke open.

In 1995 he published Power vs. Force, introducing the map of consciousness — a logarithmic scale from 20 (shame) to 1000 (enlightenment) calibrated through kinesiology. Whether you accept the methodology or not, the framework itself became one of the clearest vocabularies in modern spiritual work for the difference between force and power.
He wrote eleven more books over the next seventeen years, teaching weekend seminars until the end. He died in 2012 at 85. His students describe him as a man whose presence did most of the work.

people.name: Dr. Joe Dispenza
people.bio: Neuroscientist and meditation teacher whose progressive workshops document measurable physiological and psychological transformation through meditation.
life_story: Joe Dispenza trained as a chiropractor, completing a Bachelor of Science at Evergreen State College before earning his Doctor of Chiropractic degree from Life University. In 1986, a cycling accident left him with six broken vertebrae; he declined the recommended spinal surgery and instead used sustained mental visualisation to work towards his own recovery. That experience reoriented his thinking permanently, pointing him towards questions about the relationship between mind, body, and measurable physical change that would drive his subsequent research and writing.

Dispenza's central contribution has been to draw on neuroscience, epigenetics, and quantum physics to construct a working account of spontaneous remission — cases in which people recover from illness without conventional medical explanation. His books, including Evolve Your Brain, Breaking the Habit of Being Yourself, You Are the Placebo, and the New York Times bestseller Becoming Supernatural, work through this framework systematically. Beginning in 2012, he also began collecting data at his advanced workshops, producing a body of research into measurable physiological and psychological changes in participants practising his meditation techniques.

Dispenza continues to lecture and run multi-day residential retreats globally, alongside corporate consultancy work. His foundational teachings are available through a Progressive Online Course, and his books remain widely read across the fields his work addresses. The research strand initiated at the 2012 workshops is ongoing, with data gathered from retreat participants used to support and refine his published findings. His work sits at the intersection of self-directed healing and mainstream scientific literature on neuroplasticity and epigenetics — a position he has occupied and continued to develop for more than two decades.

people.name: Drunvalo Melchizedek
people.bio: Brought the Merkaba meditation and the Flower of Life geometry into popular esoteric teaching through workshops he ran from the 1980s onward. His two-volume Ancient Secret series remains the entry point for sacred-geometry students.

people.name: Eben Alexander
people.bio: Harvard-trained neurosurgeon who fell into a week-long coma from bacterial meningitis in 2008 and emerged with a detailed near-death experience. Proof of Heaven (2012) was the first NDE account from a working brain scientist.

people.name: Eckhart Tolle
people.bio: Author of The Power of Now, whose teaching on present-moment awareness brought non-dual consciousness into mainstream Western spirituality. A living transmission of what Osho and Krishnamurti pointed to.
life_story: Born Ulrich Tolle in 1948 in Lünen, Germany. A difficult childhood between Germany and Spain, then a brilliant academic career — University of London, research scholar at Cambridge — and severe, lifelong depression.

At twenty-nine, in a London flat, he had a sudden and apparently irreversible shift in consciousness. He could not function in the academy afterwards. For two years he mostly sat on park benches. Then, slowly, he began to speak to small groups about what had happened.

The Power of Now (1997) grew out of those talks. A New Earth (2005) became an Oprah Book Club selection and introduced millions to present-moment teaching. He lives in Vancouver. The practice is the same one he described on those benches.

people.name: Edgar Cayce
people.bio: The Sleeping Prophet — 20th-century American psychic whose trance readings produced some of the most extensive bodies of channeled material on Earth: health diagnoses, past lives, Atlantis, Jesus. His Association for Research and Enlightenment holds the archive.
life_story: Edgar Cayce was a 20th-century American whose practice centred on entering a self-induced trance state from which he would respond, at length, to questions put by attendants. These sessions — known as readings — addressed subjects ranging from medical diagnosis to theology, with Cayce reporting little conscious recall of what was said once he returned to waking. Over several decades, the transcribed sessions accumulated into one of the largest bodies of recorded material of its kind, attracting attention from people seeking health guidance as well as those drawn to its wider metaphysical claims.

The readings ranged across three principal areas: physical health, offering diagnostic assessments and dietary guidance for individual conditions; questions of past lives and reincarnation; and accounts of ancient civilisations, principally Atlantis, alongside detailed commentary on the life of Jesus. Published works drawn from the transcripts — including collections on diet and health and a commentary on the Book of Revelation — extended the material into book form, making it accessible to readers without direct access to the archive. The resulting body of work is among the most extensively documented in its tradition.

The Association for Research and Enlightenment holds the archive and has kept the readings in active circulation for close to a century. It publishes collections, maintains a programme of events, and supports an ongoing community of practitioners and researchers engaging with the material. Works attributed to Cayce, or compiled from his readings, remain in print and are available through the Association's collections and through general booksellers. The archive — preserved, indexed, and made publicly accessible — stands as an unusually thorough record of one practitioner's sustained output across health, history, and scriptural interpretation.

people.name: Edwin Abbott
people.bio: Victorian schoolmaster and theologian whose 1884 Flatland is a satire of Victorian class structure dressed as a tour of two-dimensional space. Still the cleanest introduction in print to thinking about dimensions higher than three.
life_story: Edwin Abbott Abbott was born on 20 December 1838 in England. He worked as a schoolmaster and theologian — two vocations that placed him at the junction of formal instruction, structured reasoning, and questions about the limits of what minds, shaped by their circumstances, are able to perceive. Both concerns find their way into his writing. In 1884, at forty-five, he published Flatland: A Romance of Many Dimensions, the short work for which he is best remembered.

Flatland follows a Square living in a two-dimensional world who first attempts, without success, to persuade the ruler of one-dimensional Lineland that a second dimension exists, and who is then himself visited by a Sphere from three-dimensional Spaceland. Abbott framed the book as a mathematical satire and religious allegory, and also as a portrait of Victorian social rigidity: the Square's world is organised by strict hierarchy, and its inhabitants are constitutionally unable to imagine what lies outside it. As more dimensions enter the scene, the story's pressure on fixed thought — and the inhuman behaviour it produces — intensifies.

Abbott died on 12 October 1926, at the age of eighty-seven, having spent his career as schoolmaster and theologian. Flatland has remained in continuous circulation since its first publication, valued both as a tool for thinking about spatial dimensions and as a document of Victorian social criticism. More than a century after it appeared, it is still considered useful in approaching questions of space and dimension, and still read as a commentary on what rigid hierarchy does to the imaginative range of those held within it.

people.name: Eileen Caddy
people.bio: Co-founded the Findhorn Foundation in Scotland in 1962 with her husband Peter and Dorothy Maclean after years of practising 'inner listening'. Findhorn became one of the longest-running intentional communities in Europe; Opening Doors Within is her daily-guidance distillation.

people.name: Eileen McKusick
people.bio: Sound therapist and researcher whose Biofield Tuning method uses tuning forks to map and clear the human biofield. Her evidence-gathering approach treats subtle energy as measurable — unusual, rigorous, and deeply effective in practice.

people.name: Elizabeth Kolbert
people.bio: Staff writer at The New Yorker since 1999 whose 2014 Sixth Extinction won the Pulitzer for general non-fiction. Made the scale of human-caused species loss legible without turning the reader away.

people.name: Emily Spivack
people.bio: American writer and curator whose Worn Stories (2014) collected first-person accounts from over sixty people — Cindy Sherman, Greta Lee, an inmate — about a single piece of clothing that holds a memory. The format became a Netflix series in 2021.

people.name: Emma Grede
people.bio: Co-founder and CEO of Good American, co-founder of SKIMS, founding partner of Savage X Fenty. First Black woman guest Shark on Shark Tank. Her bet: inclusivity — across sizing, race, and access — is a billion-dollar market, not a compromise. Proof that conscious business and category-leading scale aren't opposed.
life_story: Born 1982 in Plaistow, East London, to a Jamaican seamstress mother who raised her and her three sisters. Left school at sixteen, worked her way up through the fashion and celebrity-events industry, and by her late twenties was running her own talent agency.

In 2016 she co-founded Good American with Khloé Kardashian — a denim brand built around inclusive sizing, which grossed over a million dollars on launch day. Co-founded SKIMS with Kim Kardashian in 2019. Founding partner of Savage X Fenty with Rihanna.

First Black woman to appear as a guest Shark on Shark Tank. Her thesis — that inclusion across race, size, and access is a billion-dollar market rather than a compromise — has been proven out at category-leading scale across three brands. Proof that conscious business and commercial dominance are not opposites.

people.name: Eric Pearl
people.bio: Chiropractor in Los Angeles whose practice in 1993 began producing what patients described as unfamiliar healing sensations. The Reconnection (2001) outlined the energy-work modality he has since taught to over 100,000 practitioners worldwide.

people.name: Eric Raymond
people.bio: Open-source advocate whose 1997 essay The Cathedral and the Bazaar gave Netscape the framework to release Mozilla's source code, sparking the dotcom-era open-source wave. Maintainer of the Jargon File since 1990.

people.name: Erin Claire Jones
people.bio: Brings Human Design into business, leadership, and teams. Known for making HD practical and applicable to work and relationships. Her newsletter is one of the most-read in the HD space.
life_story: Erin Claire Jones built her practice around a single conviction: that Human Design could be made genuinely useful in everyday life rather than simply interesting as a theoretical system. Over the past decade she developed an approach grounded in practical application, bringing the framework into the contexts where people most often seek direction—career decisions, relationships, and the ordinary choices that accumulate into a life. Where much of the field leaned towards elaborate interpretation, her method emphasised immediate applicability, and a large following grew around that difference.

Her book How Do You Choose?, published by HarperCollins, set out the methodology in full: a hands-on guide to using Human Design for empowered decision-making across every area of life. Alongside the book, she developed coaching programmes, online courses, and personalised guides that carried the same framework to hundreds of thousands of people worldwide. The effect was to move Human Design—for many of her readers—from something they found curious to something they could act on within days of encountering it.

Jones continues to teach through her coaching practice, courses, and digital products, and her newsletter has become one of the most widely read in the Human Design space. Alongside personal alignment work, she applies the framework to business and organisational settings—leadership, team dynamics, and workplace decision-making. After a decade of consistent output, the body of work she has assembled—guides, programmes, and the HarperCollins title—now functions as one of the more substantial entry points for people approaching Human Design practically for the first time.

people.name: Ernest Holmes
people.bio: Founded the Religious Science movement in 1927 and wrote The Science of Mind, the field's textbook, the same year. Creative Mind and Success is the shorter applied volume that introduced his New Thought students to working with mental law.
life_story: Ernest Shurtleff Holmes was born on 21 January 1887 on a small farm near Lincoln, Maine, the youngest of nine sons. His mother, a schoolteacher, read aloud from the King James Bible each evening, and philosophy and religion shaped the family's reading from the start. At fifteen he left for Boston; between 1908 and 1910 he enrolled at the Leland Powers School of Expression, where he encountered Mary Baker Eddy's Science and Health alongside the writings of Emerson, Ralph Waldo Trine, and Phineas Quimby. In 1912 he moved to Southern California, discovered the Metaphysical Library in Los Angeles, and extended his reading to Thomas Troward and other New Thought writers.

Holmes completed Creative Mind and Success in 1918 — published the following year — setting out the argument that the Universal Mind is the only mind there is, pressing itself around each person's thought and returning it transformed. He framed this not as doctrine but as a practical principle open to any individual. In 1927 he launched Science of Mind magazine, and in 1938 published The Science of Mind, the movement's systematic text. Together, these works established Religious Science as a coherent school within the broader New Thought tradition and gave it an institutional foundation that outlasted his own lifetime.

Holmes continued writing and teaching, publishing further titles including This Thing Called You in 1948. He died in 1960. Science of Mind magazine, which he founded in 1927, has remained in continuous publication, and his major books stay in print. The Religious Science movement he built carries on through organisations such as Centers for Spiritual Living. His central contention — that the creative power of a universal mind is accessible to each individual — remains the organising principle of that tradition.

people.name: Ervin Laszlo
people.bio: Hungarian philosopher of science and twice-nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize who founded the Club of Budapest in 1993. Has spent the last three decades arguing for an Akashic-field theory — that information is conserved in the fabric of the universe itself.

people.name: Esther Hicks
people.bio: Channels the non-physical collective known as Abraham since 1985. With her late husband Jerry Hicks she transmitted the teachings to millions — the core source of the modern Law of Attraction tradition. Part of the FRQNCY voice lineage.

channels.name: Abraham
channels.description: A collective of non-physical intelligence channeled through Esther Hicks. The most-published voice in the contemporary Law of Attraction tradition — transmissions on alignment, emotional guidance, and deliberate creation.

life_story: Born 1948 in Coalville, Utah. Married Jerry Hicks, a former Amway salesman and seeker, in 1980. Together they spent the early years of their marriage reading Seth, Napoleon Hill, and Jane Roberts — trying to understand how reality actually responds to thought.

In 1985 Esther began to channel a non-physical collective who introduced themselves as Abraham. For the next twenty-five years she and Jerry held workshops across the US, recording hundreds of sessions that became the source material for the modern Law of Attraction movement. The Secret (2006) drew directly from their work.

Jerry died in 2011. Esther has continued teaching. The material itself — deliberate creation, emotional guidance scale, the idea that feeling is the indicator — is woven deeply into the FRQNCY voice lineage, whatever one makes of the channeling.

people.name: Florence Scovel Shinn
people.bio: American illustrator turned metaphysical teacher whose 1925 The Game of Life and How to Play It distilled New Thought into a tone — practical, witty, almost coaching — that anticipated by ninety years how the genre would eventually be written.

people.name: Francesc Miralles
people.bio: Spanish novelist and essayist who co-wrote the 2016 international bestseller Ikigai with Héctor García after fieldwork in the Okinawan village of Ogimi. Translated the Japanese reason-for-being concept for a global readership.

people.name: Frederic Laloux
people.bio: Former McKinsey associate partner whose 2014 Reinventing Organizations profiled twelve self-managing companies — Buurtzorg, Patagonia, Morning Star — and gave the post-hierarchical workplace movement a shared vocabulary.

people.name: Fritjof Capra
people.bio: Austrian-born physicist whose Tao of Physics (1975) drew the parallels between quantum physics and Eastern mysticism that a generation had been waiting for. His subsequent systems-theory work extends into ecology, biology, and economics.
life_story: Fritjof Capra was born in Austria and trained as a physicist. The conceptual upheavals of twentieth-century science — quantum mechanics and relativity having displaced the classical certainties of Newtonian mechanics — opened questions about the nature of matter and reality that the discipline rarely paused to examine on its own terms. Capra's early thinking drew him toward Eastern philosophical and contemplative traditions, where he found frameworks that appeared to address precisely the relational, participatory quality that modern physics had uncovered. That intersection became the organising concern of his early writing.

The Tao of Physics, published in 1975, drew systematic parallels between the findings of quantum and relativistic physics and the foundational concepts of Eastern philosophical and contemplative thought. The book found readers well beyond academic science, shifted how many people understood the relationship between science and philosophy, and helped open a sustained conversation about the limits of the mechanistic worldview. The Turning Point extended the project, examining how a systemic perspective might reframe the interconnected social, ecological, and economic pressures of the late twentieth century.

Capra's subsequent work moved deeper into systems theory — the study of living networks, ecological processes, and the self-organising dynamics that cut across biology, economics, and cognition. The Systems View of Life, co-authored with Luisi, synthesised this body of research into a comprehensive framework and has been adopted across disciplines ranging from microbiology and cognitive psychology to cultural anthropology and macroeconomics. His writing and public engagement continue through fritjofcapra.net, where the systems perspective he has spent decades elaborating remains the central concern.

people.name: Gabor Maté
people.bio: Hungarian-Canadian physician who spent twelve years working with addiction in Vancouver's Downtown Eastside. When the Body Says No (2003) made the clinical case that chronic suppression of emotion shows up later as autoimmune disease, cancer, and ALS.

people.name: Gary Zukav
people.bio: Former Green Beret and Harvard graduate whose 1979 Dancing Wu Li Masters won the American Book Award for science writing. The Seat of the Soul (1989) turned to authentic-power teaching that became the spine of his next four decades of work.

people.name: Georg Kell
people.bio: Founding director of the United Nations Global Compact, the worlds largest corporate sustainability initiative. Co-edited The Age of Sustainable Development.

people.name: George Green
people.bio: Former investment banker and USAF veteran who published the Pleiadian-channeled Handbook for the New Paradigm trilogy — available free online and read by millions. His Project Camelot interviews are essential: a man who moved money at the highest levels, who walked away, and who spent his final decades broadcasting what he knew.
life_story: George Green served in the United States Air Force, an experience that included a reported encounter with craft of unknown origin stored in a remote hangar at Edwards Air Force Base. After leaving the military, he moved into corporate banking and large-scale construction — what he later described as 'playing monopoly' at the upper levels of American finance. That combination of insider proximity and growing disenchantment with the structures he worked within would shape the direction of the work he eventually turned to.

Green is best known for the Handbook for the New Paradigm trilogy — a series of texts presented as messages channelled through him by the Pleiadians, intended for what he called the 'ground crew.' The books circulate freely online and have been read by millions worldwide. His interviews for Project Camelot, recorded in Spokane, Washington in 2008, gave those ideas a wider hearing: a former banker speaking about covert structures, off-planet contact, and the gap between what he had witnessed in finance and what is publicly understood about global power.

Green spent his later years distributing these ideas widely — through recorded interviews, public lectures, and the ongoing free availability of the trilogy online. The Project Camelot recordings remain among the most circulated of his appearances: a long conversation about banking, aerospace, and the nature of the information he felt compelled to share. The Handbook for the New Paradigm has never been placed behind a paywall. His work continues to circulate in the informal networks it was always aimed at.

people.name: George S. Clason
people.bio: American businessman who in 1926 published a series of parables set in ancient Babylon to teach personal finance to bank customers. The Richest Man in Babylon distilled wealth-building to seven habits that still get taught a century later.
life_story: George Samuel Clason was born on 7 November 1874 in Louisiana, Missouri. He attended the University of Nebraska and served in the United States Army during the Spanish-American War. In the early years of the twentieth century he turned to commerce, founding the Clason Map Company in Denver, Colorado. The company published the first road atlas of the United States and Canada, expanding to offices in Chicago and Los Angeles as the automobile age opened demand for navigational print. That instinct for practical, widely distributed information would carry directly into his later writing.

In 1926 Clason began issuing a series of pamphlets on thrift and financial management, each built around parables set in ancient Babylon. The device — concrete fictional characters working through debt, saving, and investment — made the principles accessible without requiring readers to navigate economic theory. Banks and insurance companies distributed the pamphlets widely, reaching millions of households. They were later collected and published as The Richest Man in Babylon, a volume that distilled a simple sequence: pay yourself first, live within your means, put money to work.

Clason spent his later years in Napa, California, and died in 1957. The book assembled from those pamphlets never went out of print. It remains on personal-finance reading lists nearly a century after the first pamphlet appeared, recommended by financial advisers who find the Babylonian parable format easier to pass on than technical instruction. The core arguments — save a portion of everything you earn, avoid debt, invest patiently — continue to circulate largely unchanged, in editions published by Penguin Random House among others.

people.name: Geshe Michael Roach
people.bio: American-born Tibetan Buddhist monk and businessman whose Diamond Cutter teachings bridge ancient Buddhist wisdom with modern business practice. His work reframes karmic mechanics as the operating principle of sustainable wealth.
life_story: American-born, Geshe Michael Roach became a Tibetan Buddhist monk before entering commercial life as one of the founders of Andin International Diamond Corporation, a jewellery business launched with fifty thousand dollars in starting capital. The combination — monastic training alongside direct involvement in building a company — shaped a body of teaching grounded in both classical Buddhist texts and hands-on entrepreneurial experience. His central premise, drawn from that dual position, is that the mechanics of karma describe how value actually moves through businesses and relationships.

His best-known book, The Diamond Cutter, layers a translation of selections from the Diamond Sutra alongside Tibetan commentary and his own teaching, using Andin's growth — from fifty thousand dollars to over a hundred million in annual sales — as worked example. A subsequent book, Karmic Management, compressed the argument into eight steps: that helping suppliers, customers, and even competitors become successful is the operative mechanism of durable business results. Both works reframe Buddhist logic not as metaphor but as a functional account of cause and effect in commercial life.
